video_title: Steady Global Economic Growth in 2027 Outlook But Risks Tilted to Downside
gist: Goldman Sachs' Jan Hatzius and Dominic Wilson see a 'remarkably unremarkable' 2.7% global growth year in 2026 (despite the Iran war, tariffs and Fed hikes) rolling into a similar 2.8% baseline for 2027, supported by front-loaded AI capex and oil easing toward ~$80, with core PCE falling to ~2.4% and the Fed, ECB and BoE hiking less than markets price. Risks are tilted to the downside (renewed Middle East escalation, fiscal/bond-yield stress centered on the French election, and an AI-investment peak); the market call is positive but lower equity returns, the best bond-return setup since 2020, a softer dollar vs. yen and yuan, and more hedging (options, energy, duration).

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs expects 2.7% world GDP growth in 2026, in line with potential, and a similar 2.8% baseline for 2027.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Steady trend growth baseline supports risk assets absent shocks.
insights.quote: We are on track for growth of 2.7%

insights.claim: The oil-price impact of the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz disruptions was smaller than expected because of pipeline redirection, dark and escorted flows through the strait, and higher price elasticity of oil demand in places like China.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Supply workarounds have capped oil upside; escalation risk remains but the physical market adapted.

insights.claim: 2026 growth was boosted by expansionary fiscal policy (the US 2025 fiscal bill, Germany's defense and infrastructure program, and Asian fuel subsidies) and by AI investment worth about 0.5% of global GDP.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Fiscal and AI capex were the two growth engines; both are expected to fade, so watch for the handoff.

insights.claim: The AI investment growth boost is very unevenly distributed: very large in East Asia, especially Taiwan and Korea, moderate in the US and much smaller elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Taiwan and Korea macro and equity markets are most leveraged to the AI capex cycle and its eventual peak.
insights.quote: large growth boost in East Asia, especially Taiwan

insights.claim: In 2027 the financial-conditions boost will fade into a moderate negative, fiscal impulse turns neutral, AI investment growth will be front-loaded early in the year and fade later, and oil declining toward about $80 should lift real household income growth.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Growth momentum likely strongest in H1 2027; consumer real income is a 2027 tailwind.

themes.theme: Downside risks: oil, fiscal, AI peak

insights.claim: Fiscal policy is on an unsustainable path in the US, to a lesser degree the UK, and especially in the euro area and France, and the April-May French presidential election could trigger bond-yield spikes that tighten broader financial conditions.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: French OATs and euro-area spreads are a key 2027 risk event; consider hedges into the election.

insights.claim: Downside risks to the AI investment path include regulatory and political pushback against data center investment, semiconductor and especially memory shortages that send nominal spending into price rather than volume, and an earlier-than-expected saturation of the AI capital stock.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Memory shortages mean AI capex dollars may inflate chip prices (bullish memory pricing) while adding less to real GDP.
insights.quote: the increase in nominal spending could end up

insights.claim: Goldman's baseline does not see an AI capex demand slowdown until 2028-2029, but the timing is hard to call.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure demand looks secure through 2027 per GS; the peak debate is about 2028+.

insights.claim: The oil risk premium (how far oil trades above fundamentals) was about $30 a few weeks ago on post-midterm escalation fears and is now close to zero, leaving the market more vulnerable and possibly underpricing the risk of renewed escalation.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: With no oil risk premium left, energy upside hedges are cheap relative to tail risk.
insights.quote: We're close to zero on the risk premium now.

insights.claim: The AI investment cycle matters more for markets than for the macroeconomy because its contribution to US capex, earnings and market value is much larger than its contribution to GDP growth.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Equity indices are more exposed to an AI-capex peak than the economy is; macro resilience may not protect markets.

insights.claim: A peak in growth rates (a second-derivative turning point) historically matters more for markets than the level of growth, because it caps the upside of return distributions even if growth stays strong.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Watch the rate of change in AI capex and earnings growth, not just levels, for equity timing.

insights.claim: AI infrastructure producers have been de-rating for a few months, making valuations less demanding, so the focus shifts to whether elevated S&P 500 earnings as a share of GDP are sustainable as the investment cycle peaks.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Earnings sustainability, not multiples, is the key 2027 debate for AI infrastructure stocks.

insights.claim: Goldman's base case is a benign AI transition with a baton pass of benefits from infrastructure providers to hyperscalers and the broader economy, supported by still-positive capex and earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Rotation from AI infrastructure suppliers toward AI adopters and hyperscalers is the favored 2027 trade.
insights.quote: there may be a kind of baton-passing from the

insights.claim: Goldman's mainline expects positive equity returns in 2027 that are less dramatic than the last three years, positive bond returns, slight credit underperformance and flattish to slightly negative commodity returns.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Lower expected equity returns and better bond returns argue for a more balanced allocation.

insights.claim: US unemployment has held at 4.1-4.2% since June and is expected to stay in that range in 2027 given growth near the 2-2.5% potential rate.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: No recession signal in labor data under the baseline.

insights.claim: Goldman now sees a broadening correlation across industries between higher AI adoption and slower employment growth and somewhat higher unemployment, which it was not seeing a year or two ago.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: AI labor displacement is now measurable; a new downside risk to consumption and a driver of lower yields.
insights.quote: industries between higher AI adoption and slower

insights.claim: Based on historical positive productivity shocks, Goldman expects AI to cause a temporary, frictional rise in the unemployment rate of about half a percentage point in the 2028 to early-2030s period.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: AI job displacement could pressure Fed policy toward easing later in the decade.

insights.claim: Tariff pass-through still contributes about 40 basis points to US core PCE inflation, and together with energy pass-through (e.g. airline fares via jet fuel) explains most of core PCE's overshoot in the low 3s versus the 2% target.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: The inflation overshoot is mostly transitory per GS, supporting a less hawkish rate path than priced.
insights.quote: that's still contributing about 40 basis points

insights.claim: Goldman expects US core PCE to fall to about 2.4% by end-2027 as tariff pass-through evaporates in early 2027, oil's year-on-year change turns benign from March-April when the war's outbreak is lapped, and nominal wage growth decelerates to the low-to-mid 3s.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Disinflation in 2027 is a tailwind for bonds and rate-sensitive assets.

insights.claim: US inflation risks are tilted to the upside mainly because commodity strategists' upside oil scenario is much further from baseline than the downside scenario; AI-related price increases are another upside risk.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Energy is the key inflation tail; hedging oil also hedges inflation surprise.

insights.claim: The Fed hiked in September, will almost certainly hike 25bp (not 50bp) in December, and Goldman expects one more hike in early 2027, more likely March than January, capping tightening below what markets price.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Fade market pricing of an extended Fed hiking cycle; front-end rates may offer value.

insights.claim: Markets price more aggressive hikes than Goldman expects from the ECB (one December hike, further move in 2027 not baseline) and the Bank of England (one hike in early 2027), because the inflation pressures are temporary.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: Receive European and UK front-end rates versus market pricing.

insights.claim: The Bank of Japan is the outlier: Goldman expects three more hikes to a 2% terminal rate, at or slightly above market pricing.
insights.speaker: Jan Hatzius
insights.so_what: BoJ tightening supports the yen and is a contrast to other central banks.

insights.claim: Government bonds were risk-additive in 2026 (yields up as equities fell), but higher starting yields plus a gradual yield decline give the best expected bond return environment since 2020.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Add duration: higher carry plus potential capital gains in 2027.
insights.quote: we've seen it since 2020 on the forecasts.

insights.claim: The balance of risks for yields is shifting from inflation and policy shocks toward growth risks (AI investment slowdown, AI job losses, financial stress from higher rates, sovereign risk in France), so bonds are regaining their value as an equity diversifier, especially at longer horizons.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Long-duration bonds become a better hedge against equity drawdowns in 2027.

insights.claim: The dollar has been range-bound near the top of its range in 2026 on the energy shock and Fed tightening, and Goldman expects modest softening in 2027, most clearly against the undervalued Japanese yen and Chinese yuan.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Short USD versus JPY and CNY is the cleanest FX expression of the baseline.

insights.claim: The euro remains a funding currency in the near term because of energy risk and the French election.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Avoid funding trades in yen/yuan with euro longs until French election risk clears.

insights.claim: Part of the dollar's premium comes from US tech exceptionalism and equity inflows, so a fading AI investment impulse could weaken the dollar more than Goldman forecasts, making the dollar more cyclical around the AI theme.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: The dollar is now partly an AI trade; AI-capex disappointment would hit both US equities and USD.
insights.quote: Part of the premium that we've built into the

insights.claim: Wilson recommends structural diversification via bonds and energy (energy still has portfolio value despite slightly negative baseline returns because of the upside tail), and explicit hedging with equity options since index volatility is low and more likely to rise.
insights.speaker: Dominic Wilson
insights.so_what: Buy cheap equity index optionality and energy upside hedges; add duration for growth-risk protection.
insights.quote: equity index volatility has stayed relatively low.
